problem:
Special Numbers

Characterize the numbers r for which the sequence floor(n*r) contains a homogeneous linearly recurrent subsequence.

framings.reframing: View sampled values b_k = floor(n_k r) as a parametric signal. A homogeneous linear recurrence means the samples admit an annihilating filter and a low-rank Hankel lift, exactly the setting of Prony and finite-rate-of-innovation reconstruction.
framings.key_insight: Prony-style theory says exact annihilation is equivalent to very small spectral support. For Beatty data, that would force the rounding carry along the selector to behave like a finite exponential model rather than like generic phase noise.
framings.suggested_technique: Use Prony's method, annihilating filters, and low-rank Hankel matrix tests.
framings.mapping_back: Search plausible selector sequences n_k and test whether floor(n_k r) yields vanishing Hankel minors or a short annihilating filter; persistent rank growth rules out recurrent subsequences.

framings.reframing: The graph of floor(n r) is a rasterized line of slope r. Asking for a linearly recurrent subsequence becomes asking whether a digital straight line contains an infinite self-similar staircase whose step pattern can be generated by a fixed transducer or substitution.
framings.key_insight: Bresenham-style digitization and the Christoffel or Freeman-code viewpoint separate true slope from rounding state. A recurrent subsequence would have to be a genuine self-embedding of the staircase, not just another locally balanced patch.
framings.suggested_technique: Use Christoffel-word decompositions, Freeman-code transducers, and Bresenham error-state analysis.
framings.mapping_back: Translate floor(n r) into its step word and test whether an induced subsequence is transducer-stable or substitution-stable; those selectors identify slopes with real geometric self-similarity.

framings.reframing: Interpret floor(n r) as cumulative service or release times in a weighted scheduler. A recurrent subsequence is then a class of jobs whose service epochs obey a fixed recurrence, analogous to the highly regular backbones sought in pinwheel schedules or smooth weighted round robin.
framings.key_insight: Scheduling theory distinguishes mere fairness from low-jitter service. The question becomes whether Beatty timing hides an infinite low-jitter service skeleton, which is much stricter than ordinary density or fairness constraints.
framings.suggested_technique: Model the selector as a pinwheel or weighted-round-robin schedule and use service-gap bounds or density tests.
framings.mapping_back: If every candidate selector produces unavoidable jitter beyond any fixed recurrence envelope, then floor(n r) has no homogeneous recurrent backbone; if a low-jitter selector exists, its gap pattern gives the recurrence candidate.

framings.reframing: Treat floor(n r) as an irregular address stream. A homogeneous recurrent subsequence is exactly the part of the stream that a delta-correlation or irregular-stream prefetcher could learn with a tiny predictor state.
framings.key_insight: Work on delta correlating prediction tables and irregular stream buffers shows that some irregular traces can be linearized into a hidden structural address space. That suggests testing whether Beatty traces contain a compressible predictor-friendly substream rather than a genuinely irreducible one.
framings.suggested_technique: Use delta-correlation prediction tables, irregular stream buffers, or learned access-pattern models to mine candidate selector sets.
framings.mapping_back: Any subsequence consistently predicted by a short delta model is a concrete recurrence candidate; if no selector makes the stream predictor-compressible, that is empirical evidence against recurrent subsequences.

framings.reframing: Read floor(n r) through the rotation-number lens of circle maps. A recurrent subsequence becomes a set of return times that behaves like a mode-locked branch or renormalizable skeleton inside an irrational rotation.
framings.key_insight: Mode locking organizes dynamics through Farey trees, devil's staircases, and renormalization. The original problem becomes whether an irrational slope supports an infinite renormalization pattern strong enough to force exact constant-coefficient recurrences on selected returns.
framings.suggested_technique: Use circle-map renormalization, Farey-tree organization of return times, and mode-locking scaling laws.
framings.mapping_back: Test whether candidate selectors n_k line up with continued-fraction or Farey renormalization scales where return maps nearly repeat; only slopes with genuine renormalization symmetry should survive.

framings.reframing: Treat n -> floor(n r) as cumulative spike count or spike timing under a periodically driven integrate-and-fire model. A recurrent subsequence is a spike-train skeleton with exact renewal-like structure.
framings.key_insight: Integrate-and-fire models use firing maps, displacement maps, and phase locking to separate periodic from quasiperiodic spiking. The Beatty question becomes whether some spikes form an exactly reproducible firing itinerary even when the full train is only quasiperiodic.
framings.suggested_technique: Analyze firing maps and interspike-interval return maps for phase-locked or renewal-like subtrains.
framings.mapping_back: Convert floor(n r) to interspike gaps, then ask whether a selector makes those gaps follow a finite renewal law or exact return-map recurrence; failure of phase locking blocks homogeneous recurrence.

framings.reframing: Focus on the fractional parts {n r} as a low-discrepancy sampling problem. A recurrent subsequence would be a selector that drives these phases into a bounded-remainder pattern tight enough to make the integer parts satisfy an exact recurrence.
framings.key_insight: Bounded remainder sets and three-gap phenomena quantify how uniformly irrational rotations visit intervals. Exact recurrence needs much more: the carry term must land in a repeatable geometry along the selector, not merely stay globally balanced.
framings.suggested_technique: Use bounded remainder set criteria, three-gap or finite-gap theorems, and discrepancy estimates for irrational rotations.
framings.mapping_back: If every infinite selector still gives too much phase variation in {n_k r}, the carry term prevents any exact linear recurrence; successful candidates would have to come from bounded-remainder geometry.

framings.reframing: The lattice path (n, floor(n r)) is a one-dimensional cut-and-project pattern. A recurrent subsequence is a self-similar submodel set, analogous to the inflation-stable pieces seen in Rauzy fractals, Meyer sets, and Pisot tilings.
framings.key_insight: Quasicrystal theory ties exact self-similarity to special algebraic scales, especially Pisot inflation factors. That points toward slopes whose strip projection admits an inflation-stable window, not generic irrationals.
framings.suggested_technique: Use cut-and-project windows, Meyer-set tests, and Rauzy-fractal or beta-tile inflation analysis.
framings.mapping_back: Embed selected points (n_k, floor(n_k r)) into a model-set picture and look for an inflation or self-tiling action; absence of such geometry argues against recurrent subsequences.

framings.reframing: Reduce floor(n_k r) modulo small primes and ask whether the selected stream has low linear complexity. A homogeneous recurrence over the integers would force very short linear-feedback descriptions modulo almost every prime.
framings.key_insight: Berlekamp-Massey and linear-complexity profiles are built to expose hidden constant-coefficient recurrences. They turn the Beatty problem into a battery of modular obstruction tests instead of a purely real-variable analysis.
framings.suggested_technique: Run Berlekamp-Massey and linear-complexity-profile tests on modular reductions of candidate subsequences.
framings.mapping_back: If floor(n_k r) mod p has large linear complexity for many primes and many candidate selectors, then no short integer recurrence can underlie the subsequence; low complexity across primes flags genuine candidates.

framings.reframing: A recurrence gives identities of the form sum_i c_i floor(n_{k-i} r) = 0, so the problem can be viewed as a hidden integer-relation problem involving r, the selector values, and bounded floor errors.
framings.key_insight: PSLQ-style methods are good at detecting latent algebraic structure from high-precision numerical data. They help distinguish accidental near-cancellations from stable relations that persist across many windows.
framings.suggested_technique: Use PSLQ or LLL-based relation hunting on vectors built from candidate recurrence windows and high-precision approximations to r.
framings.mapping_back: Numerically discovered relation families suggest specific characteristic polynomials or algebraic constraints on r; failure to stabilize under precision refinement is evidence against a true recurrent subsequence.

framings.reframing: Regard floor(n r) as a long time series and a recurrent subsequence as an exact motif with algebraic, not just geometric, repeat structure. The task is to mine sparse motifs that can later be upgraded from similarity to exact recurrence.
framings.key_insight: Matrix-profile work shows how to find repeated subsequences, discords, and shapelets at scale without precommitting to a model. That makes it a strong front-end for exploring which sparse selectors are even plausible before heavy proof machinery starts.
framings.suggested_technique: Use matrix profiles and exact motif discovery to rank candidate selectors, then post-filter by exact recurrence fitting.
framings.mapping_back: Motif mining proposes the sparse index sets n_k worth testing; if no high-quality repeated skeleton appears, the search space for genuine recurrent subsequences collapses quickly.
